catalog_quote: Assignment of stress within a word appears to be influenced by a number of factors, such as the presence of affixes and etymological considerations, and cannot always be predicted by the following simple rules. The predicted patterns are found in the majority of unaffixed words but a significant number of exceptions to these stress patterns have been found. One (only) minimal pair has been found where it appears that stress may be contrastive ... Primary st~ess falls on the initial syllable in the majority of words ... Primary stress is also found on other non-initial syllables, often where the stressed syllable has an initial liquid and is closed. ... It is not possible at present to formulate precise rules to account for stress assignment in these words. ... Words of three syllables, where the second and third syllables are both open take no secondary stress ... Words of three syllabl…

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged: initial primary stress in the majority of words, CVC-sensitive secondary stress, an unruled set of non-initial-stress exceptions and one stress minimal pair) rests on the dedicated stress section (2.3, pp. 33-37) of Stokes 1982, a 415-page ANU dissertation that is the only reference-grammar-scale description of Nyigina in Glottolog 5.1. We hold the PDF and the repository scanned text; the deciding quotation was re-located verbatim at the stated pages. Web searches for Nyikina/Nyigina stress, prosody, phonology, JIPA illustrations and dissertations turned up no later phonological or instrumental study; the open Stokes & McGregor 2003 chapter was downloaded and is silent on stress. Nothing suggests a better source exists or that the classification would change, so status is well-sourced and no action is needed.
